jntgxx: «Aunque»: the mood depends on what you do with the fact
46ztvc: After «aunque», the subjunctive does not mean the fact is false or doubtful. The mood shows how you use the information you concede. If you present it as something new for the other person, you assert it, and it goes in the indicative. If you both already know it and you only mention it to move on to your answer, you can use the subjunctive. If you are talking about something that may or may not happen, and you mean "whatever happens", you use the subjunctive.

3qe8h9: Column by Inés Lucero, an agronomist, in the opinion section of a regional newspaper in Mendoza. The author and the newspaper are fictional.

Although we all know that the Andes have less snow every year, we keep arguing as if the problem were temporary.
139csgw: It is worth starting with what nobody denies. Although drip irrigation saves up to half the water, it is not within reach of every farm. Anyone who says small growers do not change out of stubbornness has not done the sums.
1782rjs: That said, however much I understand those difficulties, I do not share the conclusion some draw from them: that it is better to wait. 1upxziv: Nor am I convinced by the opposite argument, that of those who believe technology will solve everything. n021gl: Explain in 60–80 words to another student why «aunque llueve» and «aunque llueva» can both be correct. Give a context for each.
9ewlx1: Both are correct because the mood depends on what you do with the fact. If you announce that it is raining and your friend does not know, you say «aunque llueve, salgo». If you do not know whether it will rain tomorrow and you want to say you will go out whatever happens, you say «aunque llueva, salgo». The subjunctive does not mean it is false.
